newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Europe, Islamic nations criticize Israel at U.N..
newsitem.headline: Europe, Islamic nations criticize Israel at U.N..

text.p: The European Union and Islamic nations criticised Israel on Thursday over the erupting Israeli-Palestinian crisis, telling the Jewish state it must prove its commitment to Middle East peace.

Their comments, on the margins of the annual U.N. General Assembly in New York, came as U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali appealed for calm and the Security Council met to discuss what could be done to stop the killing.

Israeli troops killed 39 Palestinians and Palestinian forces shot to death 11 Israelis in running battles on Thursday, the bloodiest day in the West Bank and Gaza since Yasser Arafat set up his self-rule government.
Israel declared a state of emergency.

Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, who speaks for the 15-nation European Union as his country currently holds the EU presidency, said he had conveyed to Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy "our deepest concern in relation to the lack of momentum in the peace process."

"We emphasised very strongly and affirmatively the concern of the European Union that it was necessary for Israel to show ... a renewed commitment to the process. ... Signals need to be given by the Israeli government," he said.

British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said the deterioration in Middle East peace efforts was "very worrying," and German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said he had appealed to both sides for calm.

Spring said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu should maintain contacts with Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat to show the world that Israel would honour peace agreements reached by the previous Labour government.
"It is necessary for Israel to give a signal, to take action that will demonstrate ... that Israel remains committed to peace," Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said.

"The disturbing fact ... is that in the Arab countries in the region the credibility of the Israeli government is being questioned and its commitment to peace, and that I think is dangerous and should not be allowed to continue."
Arab anger at Netanyahu's failure to extend self-rule in the West Bank and Gaza boiled over after his Likud government opened a tunnel near the al-Aqsa and Dome of the Rock mosques.

"Matters like that should be avoided in a situation which is particularly tense and fragile. ... Great care should be taken in terms of any action that could cause incidents and loss of life," Ireland's Spring said.
Boutros-Ghali took a similar line in urging restraint.
In a statement, the U.N. secretary-general called on both sides to end the violence and to "resume in earnest negotiations that will lead to full implementation of the agreements already reached."

Islamic nations also met to discuss the crisis and issued a statement afterwards criticising Israel, calling on it to honour previous agreements and calling the opening of the tunnel "an illegal act."

"The hesitations of the Israeli government ... are paralysing (peace) efforts," Hamid Algabid of Niger, secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (OIC), told the meeting. "To question the agreements undertaken ... would be a dangerous precedent."
Farouk Kaddoumi, foreign affairs spokesman for the Palestinians, told the OIC meeting that Israel had abandoned the principle of "land for peace" in negotiations.
"The situation is deteriorating," he said."This is an inevitable outcome of the policy pursued by Israel."
